facts.title: Born from burning seaweed
facts.text: Iodine was discovered in 1811 by French chemist Bernard Courtois while making gunpowder. He treated the ash of seaweed with sulfuric acid and saw a startling violet vapor rise from the vessel. The new element was confirmed and named soon after by Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Humphry Davy.

facts.title: Named for its violet vapor
facts.text: The name comes from the Greek word 'iodes', meaning violet or purple. When solid iodine is gently heated, it skips the liquid stage at ordinary pressure and turns straight into a striking purple gas, a process called sublimation. This vivid color inspired Gay-Lussac to coin the name in 1813.

facts.title: The least reactive halogen
facts.text: Iodine sits at the bottom of the halogen group, making it the largest and least reactive of the common halogens. Because its outermost electrons are far from the nucleus and well shielded, it grabs electrons less eagerly than fluorine, chlorine, or bromine. This is why iodine can be handled as a stable solid while fluorine is a ferociously corrosive gas.

facts.title: A thyroid essential
facts.text: Your thyroid gland uses iodine to build the hormones thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which regulate metabolism, growth, and brain development. An adult needs only about 150 micrograms a day, yet a shortage causes the neck swelling known as goiter. Severe deficiency in pregnancy is the world's leading preventable cause of intellectual disability.

facts.title: Why your salt is iodized
facts.text: To wipe out iodine deficiency, governments began adding tiny amounts of potassium iodide or iodate to table salt, starting with the United States and Switzerland in the 1920s. This cheap public-health measure dramatically reduced goiter and developmental disorders worldwide. The World Health Organization still promotes salt iodization as one of the most cost-effective nutrition interventions.

facts.title: The blue starch detective
facts.text: Iodine forms an intense blue-black complex when it slips inside the helical structure of starch molecules. Chemists exploit this vivid reaction as a sensitive test for starch and for iodine itself in titrations. The color vanishes when the iodine is used up or the structure is heated, making it a handy visual signal in the lab.

facts.title: Antiseptic on the battlefield
facts.text: Tinctures and solutions of iodine have been used to disinfect wounds since the 1800s, and they saved countless lives in 19th-century surgery and wartime medicine. Modern formulations like povidone-iodine release iodine slowly, killing bacteria, viruses, and fungi while being gentler on tissue. It remains a standard surgical skin prep in hospitals today.

facts.title: Seeing inside the body
facts.text: Iodine is so good at absorbing X-rays that iodine-based compounds are injected as contrast agents to make blood vessels and organs visible on CT scans. The heavy iodine atoms block X-rays, lighting up structures that would otherwise be invisible. Separately, the radioactive isotope iodine-131 is used both to image and to treat thyroid disease and cancer.

facts.title: Mined from ancient seas
facts.text: Most of the world's iodine comes from Chile, where it is extracted from caliche, a mineral deposit in the Atacama Desert rich in sodium nitrate and iodate. Japan is the second-largest producer, drawing iodine from underground brines linked to natural gas fields. These sources trace back to iodine that accumulated in ancient marine sediments over millions of years.

facts.title: A protective dose after disaster
facts.text: During nuclear accidents, the body can mistakenly absorb radioactive iodine-131 and concentrate it in the thyroid, raising cancer risk. Taking stable potassium iodide tablets floods the thyroid with safe iodine so it cannot take up the radioactive form. Authorities distributed these pills after the Chernobyl disaster in 1986 and the Fukushima accident in 2011.
